report.headline: tokio-rs/tracing is an engineering-mature, community-trusted Rust library with excellent traditional guardrails — a deliberately engineered behavioral test harness, fast small-batch review culture, and solid CI gating — but has not yet begun adopting AI-native conventions: no agent guidance, no AI-in-the-loop automation, and only one incidental AI-assisted commit, placing it in the Assisted (L2) band with strong bones for a fast climb to L3.
strengths: A deliberately engineered, domain-specific test harness (tracing-mock, tracing-test) drives a 0.59 test-to-source ratio across 98 files — genuine behavioral rigor, not boilerplate coverage
Fast, small-batch review culture (85% PRs ≤200 lines, 21.1h median time-to-merge, 100% reviewed on sampled merges) that would make AI-generated changes easy to absorb safely once adopted
Mature CI gating (check/fmt/clippy/cargo-hack across feature-flag combinations) plus a scheduled security-audit workflow
Strong human-facing documentation (deep README, CONTRIBUTING.md, per-crate CHANGELOGs, extensive examples/) that already gives any newcomer — human or agent — real context to build from
risks: Zero machine-readable agent guidance means every AI session starts from scratch rediscovering the 15-crate workspace layout and testing conventions, capping how much can be safely delegated
Supply-chain posture is weak — unscoped workflow token permissions, 0-of-31 pinned Action references, and no SAST — a real exposure for a library depended on by thousands of downstream crates

Branch protection is nominal only (0 required approvals/status checks), so quality currently rests on maintainer discipline rather than enforced guardrails — a riskier foundation as AI-authored PRs start to appear
AI involvement in the workflow is negligible and incidental (1 of 40 PRs), so there's no established, team-wide practice yet to build AI-native conventions on top of
No AI-in-CI or review-bot automation exists, so any future AI adoption starts from zero rather than extending an existing pattern

roadmap.title: Agent guidance is essentially absent — an agent arriving fresh has no map of the workspace, build/test commands, or testing conventions to work from
roadmap.rationale: Without a CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, every agent session has to rediscover the 15-crate workspace layout, the cargo-hack feature matrix, and the tracing-mock testing DSL from scratch — which caps how much can be trusted to an agent working unsupervised, even though the underlying test harness is already strong.
explore: What would it look like to capture the workspace layout and testing conventions (tracing-mock, cargo-hack) somewhere an agent could read first?
Which parts of CONTRIBUTING.md are also the conventions you'd want an agent to follow automatically, without a human having to repeat them each time?

roadmap.title: AI isn't yet part of the review or CI loop — the one Claude-assisted PR found looks like an individual's choice rather than a team-wide pattern
roadmap.rationale: With zero AI review bots or LLM steps in CI, any AI assistance stays confined to individual contributors' local sessions rather than compounding across the team — and with 2128 total PRs against a 36% merge rate and 0.9 avg reviews/PR, there may be review-bandwidth pressure an AI first pass could help with.
explore: Is there a review bottleneck where an AI first-pass reviewer could help maintainers triage incoming PRs faster, without replacing human judgment on correctness?
What would trust in an AI reviewer look like for a low-level, widely-depended-on crate like this one?

roadmap.title: Workflow token permissions and Action references are wide open — all 3 workflows run with default (unscoped) permissions and none of the 31 Action references are pinned
roadmap.rationale: Unscoped GITHUB_TOKEN permissions plus floating Action tags is exactly the pattern that supply-chain attacks exploit, and it's inexpensive to tighten relative to the exposure it carries for a foundational crate in the Rust ecosystem.
explore: Would scoping permissions: per workflow and pinning the 31 action references to SHAs change how confidently the team would let CI (or an autonomous agent) run unattended?
Is SAST tooling like CodeQL — free for public repos — something that's been considered and set aside, or just hasn't reached the top of the list yet?

roadmap.title: There's no repeatable harness for verifying AI-generated changes — no evals/golden tests, no prompt or agent-spec library
roadmap.rationale: As AI-assisted contributions grow beyond one-off PRs, having a repeatable way to verify LLM-produced changes becomes the difference between ad hoc prompting and a trustworthy, scalable process — right now the only verification path is the existing human review.
explore: If AI-assisted contributions grow, what would the team want checked automatically before a human even looks at the change?
Would a small library of task-specific agent prompts (e.g. fixing a clippy lint, adding a tracing-mock test) be worth capturing once a pattern repeats a few times?

roadmap.title: Branch protection is protected in name but enforces nothing — 0 required approvals and no required status checks on main
roadmap.rationale: The review culture observed in practice (100% reviewed on sampled merges) currently depends entirely on maintainer discipline rather than being guaranteed by the platform — a gap that matters more, not less, once AI-generated PRs start arriving more frequently.
explore: Given merges already average close to one review each in practice, would codifying that as a required check change daily workflow, or just formalize what's already happening?
As AI-assisted PRs increase, would a required status check feel like a useful safety net or unwanted friction for this maintainer team?
